points.en: A story holds sequence, people, setting, tension and outcome, so a short label can unpack into substantial material.
An abstract phrase lacks that internal structure, so it gives less to retrieve.
Gives an example such as a story label retrieving a whole narrative, and notes that the same quality helps the congregation remember the truth attached to the story.
Memorizing fixes exact sentences, so forgetting wording can leave the preacher lost.
Internalizing means knowing where each major idea belongs and how the ideas connect, the sermon's location and direction.
With internalized structure, wording can change, illustrations move, or thoughts lengthen or shorten, without losing the way.
The manuscript develops the historical material fully (Jewish morality, Alexander and Greek culture, the Septuagint, Roman peace) and the note reduces it to a few cues.
The cue works only because the full material was studied and written first; the cue is small because the prepared thought is large.
Cites a cue such as 'Alexander / Aristotle' reopening the Greek-culture discussion.
Agrees: a preacher who knows the movements and their order can vary wording, move an illustration, or lengthen or shorten a thought without losing the sermon.
Gives the reason: the structure, not the sentences, is what has been internalized, so it frees delivery.
Adds a limit or contrast, such as a weak structure forcing the preacher to read or wander.
A cue is a personal retrieval signal tied to material the preacher himself prepared and stored, so it can mean nothing to another person.
The test is whether the cue reliably reopens the intended material; the note is revised for recognition at a glance, not readability by others.
Gives an example, such as a story label that reopens a whole narrative only for the one who prepared it.
The conventional model states a proposition and uses the illustration afterwards, as support or decoration.
In Jesus' parables the story itself carries or discloses the truth, so a story can do more than decorate.
Keeps the caution that an illustration must not eclipse biblical truth and gives a parable example.
Because structure rather than sentence order is internalized, the preacher still knows where he is and where the sermon is going.
He can place the late illustration where it serves, tie it to its idea, or let it go, then return to the next movement.
Mentions controlled freedom or staying on the road map instead of chasing the story.
Presents an actual note with a text and three main points and no more than 15 cue words in all.
Each cue is explained as what it retrieves, such as an explanation, a Scripture, an application or a story.
The note reads as a reduction of prepared material, not a replacement for preparation.
Includes at least one story cue.
A serving story is tied to its idea, advances understanding and application, and brings the truth back to mind.
An overpowering story is remembered while the truth is forgotten, drawing attention to itself or leading away from the text.
States the test (does it serve the text and advance understanding and application?) and gives an example.
The manuscript is where the sermon is developed and thought through; the reduced note is only for retrieval.
Internalization carries the structure from the page into the mind, and the cues then guide natural extemporaneous delivery.
They work together as stages, not rivals: thorough preparation makes simple cues enough for natural speaking.
